drafts.walkScript: Line 78 says Scrooge spoke "caustic and cold as ever" to the ghost. He greets it with a blunt "How now" and no kind word at all. Nothing in the scene burns like acid, and "cold" already names his chill. A blunt greeting is not careful speech either. So caustic describes his biting way of speaking, sharp and cutting in what he says.

Line 20 says Bevis "strode over the yielding sand." Mark could put "his feet into the marks Bevis left" there. Sand only holds deep marks when it gives way under each step. The marks come from that softness, but they are not what yielding means. So yielding sand is soft, and a foot sinks into it.

Lines 7 and 8 show Fogg "handing the cards to Thomas Flanagan." So the men are in the middle of a card game. Line 9 says "The discussion fell during the rubber, after which Stuart took up its thread." The rubber is what the men were doing while the talk stopped. It is a set of card games played through to the end, not the silence.

Line 23 says Fogg "threw down the cards" when his play was done. Line 24 says Stuart, "whose turn it was to deal, gathered them up." Gathering only collects the cards, so it is a step before dealing. The cards come back to Stuart so that the next game can start. So his turn to deal means it was his to give out the cards again.

Line 76 says the other players "seemed much agitated", so they were uneasy. Lines 76 and 77 say the money was not the main cause of it. Lines 77 and 78 give the real cause: "betting under conditions so difficult to their friend." They felt it might not be fair to bet on something so hard for him. So scruples are uneasy feelings about whether a thing is right.

On line 16 the speaker knows "who's tired" among the players. Line 17 adds "who's got a stitch and won't say it." Line 15 shows the players "running" for the whole game. Somebody hides a stitch, so it must be something that hurts. Line 18 names a trick, so a stitch is a sharp pain from running.

Line 22 says Rikki-tikki "sat up and put his fur in order". He had just been wrapped in cotton wool and warmed by a fire. Next he scratches himself, so he is grooming his coat. Order is the state he leaves his fur in, not the mess he starts with. Nobody commands him, so order here is a tidy state, with the fur smoothed down.

Line 54 has Rikki-tikki say "I am a stranger here." The word "here" ties it to the garden, not to how sad he feels. He then asks who Nag is, though Darzee named Nag on line 53. The birds know Nag, but Rikki-tikki does not know who lives here yet. So a stranger here is somebody new, who does not know the place.

Line 7 says the butterfly is hanging "with its wings going". Line 8 calls the pumping of the wings "the sign". Line 9 says butterflies left in the net then "get sad and start bashing themselves". So the pumping tells you what comes next for the butterfly. The sign is not a board or the card; it shows what is about to happen.

Lines 31 and 32 say one butterfly "went through the serving hatch into the kitchen." The word "through" shows the hatch is a gap something can pass along. It leads into the kitchen, so it is an opening between two rooms. The word "serving" shows food is handed through it to people. The extinguisher on line 31 is where a different butterfly landed.

Line 24 says "Jo’s hot temper mastered her". The temper is doing something to Jo, so Jo is no longer in charge. Line 25 shows the result, as she cries "in a passion of grief and anger". Shaking Amy is what the temper made her do, not what mastered means. So her temper got the better of her.

Line 60 says Laurie was "sounding the ice" as he skated. The same line gives the reason: "a warm spell had preceded the cold snap." Warm weather before the freeze could leave the ice thin in places. Line 61 has him go ahead to "see if it’s all right" before the race. So sounding means testing how solid the ice is, not where he skates.

Line 19 warns "you do not spear them", meaning the potatoes. It says a misplaced fork makes "a noise like a knife going into an apple". So spearing drives the fork into a potato, the way a knife enters an apple. The hand's width on line 18 is how to avoid it, not what it means. The fork is digging, not lifting food, so spear means push the point right through.

Line 25 says "Alan from plot fourteen" came over with a marrow. Line 1 sets the story at "the allotment", where Grandad grows potatoes. Plot fourteen has a number, so it is one patch among many there. A marrow is a vegetable, which fits a piece of ground where food is grown. Lines 25 and 26 put him at the end of the row, not on his plot.

Line 11 says "He looks paler than his wont". The words "paler than" set up a comparison between two looks. One is how he looks today, and "his wont" is the other. Line 15 shows the crowd knows his pictures, so they know his normal face. So wont means his usual way of looking, not a reason or a refusal.

Line 17 begins "But, in spite of these signs of approval". Line 18 says the people met the speaker "in silence and with sullen looks". "In silence" already says they were quiet, so "sullen" adds something more. Line 19 calls the portraits "an ironical sort of greeting", which shows ill feeling. So sullen means silently resentful, not just silent.

Line 17 says she watched "what landed on" the lid of sugar water. Line 18 sets "the slow heavy ones" against "the ones that hovered". Lines 18 and 19 say these hovered "before they settled". "Before" shows the hovering came first, and the landing came after. So hovered means stayed up in the air for a moment, not landing straight away.
